strengths: Technically sound methodology with edge-conditioned transformer and aligned functional gradients providing principled inductive bias for dense brain graphs
Comprehensive experimental validation across HCP (N=1067) and BSNIP (n=984) datasets with proper train/val/test splits and careful data leakage prevention
Thorough ablations (Table 2) and multiple complementary evaluation metrics (reconstruction, classification, distribution alignment) demonstrating each component's contribution

Novel combination of techniques addressing genuine problem (avoiding thresholding artifacts in FC graphs) with domain-specific innovations (Procrustes-aligned gradients, memory-based cross-attention decoder)
Unsupervised learning of representations that meaningfully separate cognitive states and enable downstream decoding without label supervision
Well-designed extensions (neural dynamics fusion improves cognitive decoding to 89.7%, latent diffusion enables graph generation) that validate interpretability of learned geometry
Transparent presentation with detailed hyperparameters, ablations, and honest limitations discussion; code availability promised
Neuroscientifically meaningful insights linking gradient-related latent reconfiguration to behavioral performance while demonstrating that excessive task-evoked dispersion is detrimental
weaknesses: Empirical improvements over baselines are modest (~22% reconstruction improvement over GATE, 78.6% cognitive load classification, 73.7% AUC for HC vs schizophrenia) and clinical significance remains unclear

Limited architectural novelty: edge-conditioned attention from Ma et al. (2023), functional gradients from Margulies et al. (2016), Procrustes alignment and diffusion models established; primary contribution is engineering combination rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts

Inconsistent application of gradient geometry: 20% sparsification used for gradient computation but dense FC for reconstruction objective—rationale unclear and potentially introduces bias in inductive bias

Interpretability limited: two-factor latent readout explains only R²=0.52 of variance in network metrics (Δ²={0.38, 0.14}), leaving substantial unexplained variance; no systematic probing of learned latent structure
Gradient spread proxy (Eq. 7) using range is susceptible to outliers despite post-hoc quantile robustness check; no ablation on alternative measures

Diffusion generation validation incomplete: no evaluation of neurobiological plausibility of generated graphs or validation that synthetic samples preserve known connectomic properties beyond summary statistics
Limited baseline comparisons: no simple dimensionality reduction baselines (PCA/ICA on graphs), no VAE graph autoencoders; missing 2024 work besides GRALE

Paper covers too many topics (representation, generation, cognitive decoding, interpretation) creating somewhat diffuse narrative; connections between three extensions feel disconnected rather than integrated

Experimental design limitations: only 4 random seeds, working-memory analysis uses specific partitioning with unclear generalizability, no sensitivity analysis to resting-state template choice, classification uses only logistic regression

Statistical reporting inconsistencies: task dispersion effect (β=-0.16) is statistically significant but effect size small; some results lack confidence intervals; multiple comparisons corrections not always explicit
Clinical applicability unvalidated: BSNIP results positioned as research tools only; no comparison to conventional clinical markers, no treatment-naive vs treated analysis, no longitudinal validation
Missing analyses: no cross-site validation, no robustness assessment to preprocessing variations, no investigation of why edge-conditioned attention outperforms sparse attention for this domain
